scenes.name: El underground de Londres
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En Gran Bretaña el LSD circulaba por el mismo tipo de gente que en Estados Unidos: estudiantes de arte, hipsters, bohemios y poetas, muchos llegados desde la CND. Su primera gran reunión fue la International Poetry Incarnation del Albert Hall (junio de 1965: Ginsberg, Trocchi, Burroughs, Adrian Mitchell), filmada por Peter Whitehead. En enero de 1966 John Hopkins y Steve Stollman montaron en el Marquee el primer Spontaneous Underground, intento, como los Acid Tests, de crear un entorno que se acercara a la disrupción perceptiva del LSD; el 13 de marzo, «The Trip», con el grupo de improvisación AMM y el debut en el Marquee de unos Pink Floyd que dejaban las versiones de R&B. En febrero Barry Miles y John Dunbar abrieron la librería Indica (ESP-Disk, Burroughs, Leary, Artaud, Crowley, Gurdjieff, Blavatsky), con la ayuda de Paul McCartney. En abril Miles y Hopkins repartieron en la marcha de la CND THE Global moon-edition Long Hair TIMES.

scenes.name: Protometal: volumen, distorsión y moteros
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Los precursores que aportan piezas sueltas del código: el volumen como estética (Blue Cheer, MC5), el sonido de guitarra grueso y distorsionado (los Kinks en «You Really Got Me»), la contundencia de los Who en directo (Townshend presume de que Live at Leeds engendró «ese objeto grosero y asqueroso que fue Led Zeppelin») y la iconografía motera de «Born to Be Wild» de Steppenwolf, cuyo verso «heavy metal thunder» dio nombre al género. Algunos críticos estadounidenses defienden a Iron Butterfly, Steppenwolf o Blue Cheer como primera banda de heavy. En 1971 la crítica ya usa el término: Mike Saunders, en Creem, dice que Sir Lord Baltimore domina «todos los trucos del heavy metal».

podcast.title: Collaboration with Kurt Cobain
podcast.body: In 1992, William Burroughs met and collaborated with Kurt Cobain on a spoken word piece titled "The Priest, they called him," released in 1993. Burroughs read one of his stories, accompanied by Kurt Cobain's guitar sounds. Burroughs was reportedly very pleased with the recording. "That's William Burroughs and Kurt Cobain on guitar. From 1993, with a piece called The Priest, they called him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dream Machine Invention
podcast.body: William Burroughs invented a trance-inducing device called a "dream machine," which consists of a cylinder with an internal light source that rotates, causing the light to flash exactly 10.56 times per second. The theory is that staring at these flashes induces a trance-like state, and in the 1960s, several experimenters with these machines allegedly committed suicide. "The machine consists of a cylinder with a light source inside. When he switched on the cylinder rotates, causing the light to flash at a rate of exactly 10.56 times per second."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dream Machine Recommendation to Kurt Cobain
podcast.body: After their 1992 collaboration on "The Priest, they called him," William Burroughs was so pleased that he told Kurt Cobain about his invention, the "dream machine." He then connected Cobain with Dave Woodward, a builder in San Francisco who created these machines for special clients, leading to Cobain ordering one immediately. "Burroughs was apparently so pleased with how this recording turned out that he told Kurt about the dream machine. He even fixed him up with a guy in San Francisco named Dave Woodward who built machines for special clients."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: House Fire and Theft (1996)
xref.body: In 1996, John Frusciante's house burned down. The fire originated in his painting room, likely due to the presence of paint cans and turpentine. He was awakened by the heat and escaped to a neighbor's house to call the fire department. He lost all his paintings, including two by poet William Burroughs. Most of his guitars initially survived, but were stolen after he went to New York following the fire. The only musical items that remained were his four-track demo tapes. "Most of his guitars were fine, but when John escaped to New York after the fire, somebody came in and stole them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Collaboration with William Burroughs
xref.body: In 1992, Kurt Cobain and writer William Burroughs met and collaborated on a unique spoken word piece titled "The Priest, they called him," released in 1993. Cobain contributed all the guitar sounds to the recording, complementing Burroughs' reading of his story. "In 1992, Kurt and Burroughs not only met, but collaborated on a strange spoken word piece. Kurt provided all the guitar sounds, while Burroughs read one of his stories."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Dream Machine Connection Myth
xref.body: A cult-like organization called "Friends Understanding Kurt" suggests that Kurt Cobain's death in 1994 was linked to his use of a "dream machine," a trance-inducing device invented by William Burroughs. After their 1992 collaboration, Burroughs was reportedly pleased and told Kurt about the machine, even introducing him to builder Dave Woodward in San Francisco. Kurt immediately ordered one, but Courtney Love, sensing its danger, tried to prevent its delivery. According to "Friends Understanding Kurt," Cobain used the machine for up to 72 hours at a time, and it was found just 20 feet from his body on April 8, 1994, though neither police nor the coroner investigated this connection. "The machine was found just 20 feet away from his dead body on April 8, 1994. Neither the police, nor the corner investigated the connection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
